We have carbon NMR data: chemical shifts: 169.52, 132.43, 130.27, 129.30, 126.70, 126.66, 123.57, 43.30, 26.29.

We need number of methyl (CH3) groups in the molecule. Methyl carbon typically appears around 10-30 ppm for aliphatic, but if attached to aromatic or carbonyl, shift can be higher (e.g., 30-40). Here we have two aliphatic carbons: 43.30 and 26.29. 43.30 likely a carbon attached to heteroatom (e.g., carbonyl carbon of acetyl? Actually carbonyl carbon is around 170, which we have 169.52 (likely carbonyl). So 43.30 could be a carbonyl carbon's alpha carbon (e.g., CH3 attached to carbonyl: acetyl CH3 appears ~30 ppm). 26.29 could be a methyl attached to aromatic ring (toluene) ~20 ppm. So there are likely two methyl groups.

But need to be sure: The aromatic carbons are many: 132,130,129,126,126,123. That's six aromatic carbons (maybe a phenyl). Carbonyl at 169.5 (likely ester or amide). Then aliphatic carbons: 43.3 (maybe CH2 or CH3 attached to carbonyl), 26.29 (CH3). Could there be a CH2? 43.3 could be CH2 (e.g., O-CH2). But methyl carbon is typically ~10-30. 43 is high for methyl; maybe it's a methylene attached to carbonyl (e.g., CH2-CO). But we have only one carbonyl carbon, so maybe it's an acetyl group: CH3-CO- (methyl carbon ~30). 43 is a bit high but could be due to being attached to heteroatom (e.g., O-CH3 in methyl ester appears ~52 ppm). So 43 could be O-CH3 (methyl of methyl ester). That would be a methyl. So we have at least two methyls.

Thus answer likely 2.

We could also retrieve proton NMR to confirm number of methyl signals. Let's get proton NMR.
